prompt: After `swap(x, y)` with `x = 1` and `y = 2`, what did `main` print?
hint: `swap` worked on copies.

choices.why: That is what `swap` printed inside, about its own copies `a` and `b`.
Right: the caller's variables were never touched.
Nothing assigned to `x` at all; `swap` only had copies.

choices.text: Nothing: the program fails to compile
choices.why: It compiles; assigning to a parameter is allowed.

prompt: In the bytecode of `main`, which instructions handed `x` and `y` to `swap`?
hint: They push values, not variables.

choices.text: `istore_1` and `istore_2`
choices.why: Those put 1 and 2 into `main`'s slots, before the call.

choices.text: `iload_1` and `iload_2`, then `invokestatic`
choices.why: Right: the two values were pushed and the call took them.

choices.text: `iload_0` and `istore_0`, inside `swap`
choices.why: Those run inside `swap` on its own slots, after the handover.

prompt: What is a method parameter, as far as the JVM is concerned?
hint: Lesson 5's frame.

choices.text: A local variable of the method, filled in by the caller
choices.why: Right: `swap`'s parameters were its slots 0 and 1.

choices.text: A pointer into the caller's frame, so writes go straight back
choices.why: No JVM instruction reaches another method's frame.

choices.text: A field of the class, shared by every call to the method
choices.why: Each call gets fresh parameters in a fresh frame.

choices.text: A second name for the caller's variable, as in pass by reference
choices.why: That is pass by reference, which Java does not have.

prompt: Java passes every argument by ___: the method receives a copy of what the caller's variable holds.
hint: The opposite of "by reference".

prompt: `renew(mine)` changed `mine`'s book. What did `renew` receive?
hint: What does a variable of a class type hold?

choices.text: The variable `mine` itself, under another name
choices.why: Then `replace` would have changed `mine` too, and it did not.

choices.text: A copy of the `Book` object
choices.why: A copy of the object would have been changed instead of the original; `main` saw the change.

choices.text: A copy of the reference in `mine`
choices.why: Right: two arrows to one object, so a change through either is visible to both.

prompt: After `replace(mine)`, `mine` was still *Dom Casmurro*, renewed once. What happened to the *Iracema* object?
hint: Who pointed at it when `replace` returned?

choices.text: It replaced *Dom Casmurro* on the heap, at the same address
choices.why: Nothing is replaced in place; `new` made a second object.

choices.text: It became unreachable when `replace` returned, and so garbage
choices.why: Right: only `b` pointed at it, and `b` went with the frame.

choices.text: It was copied back into `mine` and then discarded by `main`
choices.why: Nothing is copied back from a method except its return value, and `replace` returns nothing.

prompt: In `replace`'s bytecode, `astore_0` follows the construction of the new `Book`. What does it store, and where?
hint: Slot 0 of a static method is its first parameter.

choices.text: The new object, into the caller's variable `mine`
choices.why: No instruction reaches `main`'s frame.

choices.text: The reference to the new object, into `replace`'s own parameter `b`
choices.why: Right: an ordinary store into its own frame, like `istore_0` for an `int`.

choices.text: The string `Iracema`, written into the field of the book that `mine` points at
choices.why: That would be `putfield`; `astore` writes a local slot.

prompt: A method receives `Book b`. Which of these can the caller see after the method returns? Choose all that apply.
hint: Through the arrow, or to the arrow?

choices.text: `b.renewals = 5;`
choices.why: Yes: it writes a field of the shared object.

choices.text: `b = new Book("X");`
choices.why: No: it re-points the method's own copy.

choices.text: `b.title = b.title.toUpperCase();`
choices.why: Yes: the field of the shared object now holds a new string.

choices.text: `b = null;`
choices.why: No: only the method's copy becomes `null`.

prompt: Which sentence describes Java's argument passing?
hint: Section 03 has a sentence to keep.

choices.text: Primitives by value, objects by reference
choices.why: The common belief; `replace` and the swap of two strings refute it.

choices.text: Everything by reference, primitives copied
choices.why: There is no reference passing at all in Java.

choices.text: Everything by value; for an object, the value is a reference
choices.why: Right: one rule, no exceptions.

prompt: `shout(name)` runs `s = s.toUpperCase();` and `name` still prints `ana`. Why?
hint: What does `toUpperCase` return?

choices.text: It returns a new string, and `s =` re-points only the method's copy
choices.why: Right: the original string is unchanged, as strings always are.

choices.text: Strings are passed by value, unlike other objects
choices.why: Strings are passed like every other object: a copy of the reference.

choices.text: `toUpperCase` fails silently on lower-case input
choices.why: It worked; the upper-case string was simply never stored where `main` could see it.

prompt: Which experiment settles that Java does not pass objects by reference?
hint: In a language with pass by reference, one of these would have worked.

choices.text: `zero(numbers)` changing the array
choices.why: That works the same under both models, so it decides nothing.

choices.text: `empty(titles)` clearing the list
choices.why: A method call on the shared object works under both models.

choices.text: `swap(first, second)` leaving them as `AB`
choices.why: Right: by reference, the caller's two variables would have swapped.

choices.text: `increment(count)` leaving 5, since an object came back unchanged
choices.why: Suggestive, but `Integer` being immutable muddies it; the two-object swap is the clean test.

prompt: `increment(Integer n)` runs `n++`, and `count` stays 5. What did `n++` do?
hint: `Integer` is immutable.

choices.text: Changed the shared `Integer`, which `main` then cached
choices.why: No `Integer` changes; there is no method that could change one.

choices.text: Made a new `Integer` holding 6 and pointed its own `n` at it
choices.why: Right: unbox, add, box a new one, reassign the method's own copy.

choices.text: Nothing, because `++` does not work on `Integer`
choices.why: It compiles and works on the method's copy, through boxing.

prompt: Match each method body to what the caller sees afterwards.
hint: Through the reference, or to the parameter?
right_distractors: a new empty list in the caller's variable

prompt: Why does Java have no `ref` or `&` parameter syntax, as C# and C++ do?
hint: What would that syntax be for?

choices.text: Because every object parameter is already a `ref` parameter
choices.why: Then a swap of two objects would work, and line 3 shows it does not.

choices.text: Because Java has no pass by reference
choices.why: Right: a method that must give back something new returns it.

choices.text: Because `final` parameters do the same job
choices.why: `final` stops reassignment; it gives the caller nothing back.

prompt: A method has to give its caller both the smallest and the largest value of an array. How does section 05 do it?
hint: A method returns one value.

choices.text: Two `int` parameters that the method fills in
choices.why: Assigning them would change only the method's copies.

choices.text: It returns a record holding both
choices.why: Right: `MinMax(min, max)`, read with `min()` and `max()`.

choices.text: Two static fields the caller reads afterwards
choices.why: That works and shares mutable state across every call, which lesson 15 warned against.

prompt: After `sortedCopy(pages)`, `pages` was still `[256, 640, 180]`; after `sortInPlace(pages)` it was sorted. What made the difference?
hint: Which array did each one sort?

choices.text: `sortedCopy` received a copy of the array, and `sortInPlace` the array itself
choices.why: Both received a copy of the same reference; one of them cloned the array itself.

choices.text: One of them cloned the array before sorting
choices.why: Right: `values.clone()` made a second array, and only that one was sorted.

choices.text: `Arrays.sort` only changes arrays it creates itself
choices.why: It sorts whatever array it is given, as `sortInPlace` showed.

prompt: `static void replace(final StringBuilder b)` contains `b.append("!");` and `b = new StringBuilder("other");`. Which line does `javac` refuse?
hint: `final` is about the arrow, not the object.

choices.text: `b.append("!");`, because `b` is final
choices.why: `final` does not freeze the object; the call compiled.

choices.text: Both lines
choices.why: Only the assignment broke the rule.

choices.text: `b = new StringBuilder("other");`
choices.why: Right: `final parameter b may not be assigned`.

prompt: Put what happens during `replace(mine)` in order.
hint: Copy first, re-point last.
items: `replace`'s frame is created, with that reference in `b`
A new `Book` is built on the heap
`replace` returns and its frame, with `b`, is discarded

prompt: A colleague writes `void reset(Book b) { b = new Book(b.title); }` to set a book's renewals back to 0. What does the caller see?
hint: Is anything written through the reference?

choices.text: The book with 0 renewals, as intended
choices.why: The new book went into the method's copy of the arrow and was then discarded.

choices.text: The same book, with its renewals unchanged
choices.why: Right: the fix is `b.renewals = 0;`, or returning the new book.

choices.text: A `NullPointerException`, because the old book is collected
choices.why: The caller still points at the old book, so it is not garbage.

choices.text: A compile error, because a parameter cannot be reassigned
choices.why: It can, unless it is `final`; it compiles and does nothing visible.
